paras: The shooting of Perry McGee was the wounding of a Black cavalry private, wanted for killing two Black infantrymen, by a constable and an armed villager at Boonville, New York, on August 30, 1910. McGee, reported to have fired on his pursuers first, was shot in the back while in a canal, and physicians at first said he could not live. Wire accounts ran in white papers from New England to Texas, and a later report placed him alive in a Watertown hospital.

McGee was a private in Troop L of the Tenth U.S. Cavalry, one of the units at the camp of instruction at Pine Plains, or Pine Camp, near Watertown. On the night of August 29, Private Turner and Corporal Jones of the Twenty-fourth Infantry were shot and killed in a fight in the Freeman House ballroom at Great Bend, near the camp. All three were Black; the New-York Tribune reported that McGee fled the ballroom.

A Syracuse dispatch described a "free-for-all fight" after the infantrymen entered and said McGee claimed self-defense. A later item quoted McGee as saying the quarrel had started over a crap game at the camp.

According to the Utica dispatch of the Associated Press, Boonville had been warned by the military authorities at Pine Camp to look out for the fugitive. When the 8 o'clock train arrived, Deputy Sheriff Wetmore and Constable Studor saw McGee on the bumpers, and he ran up the tracks. He held off two villagers with his cavalry pistol until others joined the chase and cornered him between the canal and a knitting mill.

Pressed by the crowd, McGee jumped into the canal and, standing waist deep, turned his gun on his pursuers; when Studor told him to surrender, he fired at the constable. Studor fired back, Walter Rinkle came up with a rifle, and the two fired together, dropping McGee with two bullets in his back. Physicians said at the time that he could not live.

In the Syracuse version, McGee opened fire when ordered to halt as he left a freight train, and the officers put four bullets into his back before he jumped into the canal. The officers then drew him out and took him to the Boonville jail, "where it was said he would die."

A short item syndicated in early September reported that McGee had been taken to the city hospital at Watertown and that one bullet had struck him, "making four holes in his body." It added that army physicians found Jones shot through the heart and Turner through the lung. No report of McGee's death, of an inquiry into his shooting, or of a trial appears in the coverage, and the Morris County Chronicle reprinted the Utica account on September 6 without later news.

Only white papers carried the case. The Utica dispatch ran on August 30 in the Newark Evening Star as "Negro Soldier Slayer Is Captured With Bullets" and in the San Antonio Light and Gazette as "Murderer Is Captured." Over the next two days it ran in the Montgomery Advertiser as "Fugitive Fights Officers," in the Daily Kennebec Journal as "Soldier Shoots Soldier," and in the Burlington Weekly Free Press as "Colored Trooper Fought Pursuers," along with papers in Barre, Fargo, Los Angeles and Salt Lake City.

The Syracuse dispatch ran the same day in the Richmond Virginian as "Negro Kills Two; Caught in Water," and in the New Haven Union and Alexandria Gazette. Headlines in both versions treated the double killing as settled, the Burlington paper calling McGee the man "Who Killed Two Men," though the Syracuse text said only that it was "alleged" he had shot them. Both versions marked each soldier's race and told the Boonville shooting only from the pursuers' side.

McGee's first name appears as Perry in most copies, Berry in the Montgomery Advertiser and "Ferry" in the Burlington paper. His wounds were two bullets in the back (Utica), four bullets (Syracuse) or one bullet making four holes, the last from the Watertown report written after he reached hospital. The Utica account credited the capture to civil officers and villagers, while the Syracuse account named the sheriff and a detail of soldiers.

reader.title: Shooting of Perry McGee
bases: A deputy sheriff and a constable, joined by an armed villager and a pursuing crowd, shot a Black soldier wanted for a double killing as they tried to arrest him; he was wounded, not reported killed (A2, A3, A14).

McGee was wounded, not reported killed, and was in a Watertown hospital days later (A14); he was shot by a deputy sheriff and constable making an arrest, with a citizen joining, after he was reported to have fired on them (A2, A3).
Two separately written dispatches, from Utica (A2, A8) and Syracuse (A3, A4), agree that officers shot McGee at Boonville while capturing him, though both give only the pursuers' version.

accounts.gist: Officers spotted McGee on the train bumpers; he ran, held off villagers with his pistol, jumped into the canal and fired at Studor when told to surrender; Studor and Rinkle fired together and hit him twice in the back.

accounts.label: Syracuse dispatch
accounts.gist: Ordered to halt as he left a freight train, McGee opened fire; the officers put four bullets into his back, he jumped into the canal, was drawn out and taken to the Boonville jail; arrest credited to the sheriff and a detail of soldiers.

accounts.label: McGee's claim
accounts.gist: McGee said he acted in self-defense in the Great Bend fight and that the quarrel began over a crap game.

accounts.label: Watertown follow-up
accounts.gist: McGee was in the Watertown city hospital; one bullet had struck him, making four holes.

framing.detail: Utica AP copy ran as 'Negro Soldier Slayer Is Captured With Bullets' (Newark), 'Murderer Is Captured' (San Antonio), 'Fugitive Fights Officers' (Montgomery), 'Soldier Shoots Soldier' (Kennebec), treating the killings as established and the shooting as a capture.
Syracuse copy ran as 'Negro Kills Two; Caught in Water' (Richmond) and 'Trooper Is Arrested' (New Haven), with the body text calling the shootings 'alleged' and reporting a self-defense claim.
